item.text: {"winner":"B","confidence":"high","summary":"Candidate B is materially closer to the frozen contract because it preserves FilesService.Add and limits the behavioral change to the new Upload API. It still needs a small correction: Upload must delegate to Add instead of duplicating its request path.","reasons":["B preserves Add's existing streaming behavior, while A unconditionally reads every Add body into memory and explicitly changes its retry semantics, contrary to the requirement to preserve Add behavior.","B implements the exact Upload signature, uses multipartbody.NewFile with field \"file\", validates filename/content before requesting, and propagates helper errors.","B covers multipart encoding, no-request validation, and replay after 429. A has a stronger streamed os.File retry test, but omits explicit validation and source-reader-error tests.","B's main contract violation is localized and readily fixed by replacing the duplicated request/response block with return s.Add(ctx, body, contentType, opts...). A would require reverting broader API behavior, documentation claims, helper refactoring, and its Add retry test."],"risks_a":["Changes the established lower-level Add API from streaming to unconditional in-memory buffering, affecting memory use, timing, and reader-error behavior.","Upload calls a new private add helper rather than routing through FilesService.Add as explicitly required.","README and changelog advertise the out-of-contract Add behavior change and broaden scope unnecessarily beyond the convenience API contract."],"risks_b":["Upload duplicates Add's option handling, request construction, decoding, and error handling instead of delegating to Add, creating immediate drift risk and directly violating the routing requirement.","No test covers propagation of a source reader failure.","The retry test supplies bytes.NewReader as source content rather than an opaque streamed reader, so it less directly demonstrates the reported streamed-content scenario."]}
